newsitem.title: UK: UK's Labour promises defence review but no cuts.
newsitem.headline: UK's Labour promises defence review but no cuts.

text.p: The opposition Labour Party on Thursday promised a full-scale review of Britain's defence needs if it wins next week's election but said there would be no cuts.
Labour, whose defence policies proved major liabilities in past elections, backed the Eurofighter combat jet project and vowed not to scrap Britain's nuclear weapons.
"The defence review is a mechanism for returning stability, direction and cohesion to our armed services," said defence spokesman David Clark.
He accused the ruling Conservatives of being "haphazard, desperate and short-termist" with swingeing defence spending cuts of almost 30 percent.

Clark, making his major policy statement of the campaign for Britain's May 1 election, acknowledged that nuclear weapons had once been a contentious issue for Labour, portrayed by the Conservatives as naive socialists ready to sell out Britain.
But in a speech for the Royal United Services Institute, he said: "Labour will retain the British nuclear deterrent, Trident."
His major pledge was a definitive defence review within six months but he stressed: "It is not a device by which to make cuts to defence spending."
Calling for more cross-party consensus on defence, he said that Labour would not back out of the much delayed Eurofighter project. Britain is developing the combat jet with Germany, Italy and Spain.
He said the Eurofighter was vital to Britain's defence industry. "Labour will honour the commitment to the Eurofighter as we will all other contracts that have been signed," he said.

Labour has lost the last four elections but modernising leader Tony Blair is tipped to win this time. His party has ditched old pledges to leave the European Union, scrap Britain's nuclear weapons and abandon the arms race.
Defence was once viewed as a Conservative bastion by voters but Clark insisted that, after 18 years in power, the ruling party "have left cuts, waste and chaos in their wake."
"They have treated our armed forces with apathy, our defence industry with incompetence and squandered billions of pounds (dollars) of taxpayers' money," Clark said.
He promised to offer a fair deal to war veterans who complain of so-called Gulf War Syndrome and accused the government of lagging behind with compensation and research.

Scores of Britons who served in the 1991 Gulf War campaign following Iraq's invasion of Kuwait have complained of debilitating illness, which they believe was caused by exposure to organophosphate pesticides.
Clark said Labour would provide more doctors if necessary. "We will streamline the war pension process so that veterans do not see their claims mired in red tape," he said.
